claims.text: Enhancing coherency at FCC/BCC interfaces will reduce creep in dual-phase high-entropy-alloy coatings.
Solute enrichment at FCC/BCC interfaces will reduce creep in dual-phase high-entropy-alloy coatings.
Interface coherency and solute enrichment reduce creep by pinning dislocation motion.
Controlled annealing can selectively enhance or diminish coherency and solute segregation at FCC/BCC interphase boundaries.
TEM and atom probe tomography can confirm the targeted changes in interface coherency and solute segregation.
FCC/BCC interphase boundaries act as strong barriers to dislocation motion.
Enhanced interface coherency creates effective pinning sites.
Interfacial solute enrichment creates effective pinning sites.
The proposed interface pinning impedes diffusion-assisted dislocation climb and slip during creep.
Reduced interface coherency or chemical uniformity provides less hindrance to dislocation motion and therefore produces a higher steady-state creep rate.
Coatings with enhanced interphase characteristics will have lower steady-state creep strain rates than the baseline coatings.
Coatings with enhanced interphase characteristics will show a delayed onset of tertiary creep relative to the baseline.
The proposed mechanism is expected to operate at approximately 0.5–0.7 Tm under constant loads of approximately 60–70% of yield stress.
Interface-mediated dislocation pinning is dominant under the stated temperature and load conditions.
Grain boundaries and secondary phases may also influence the measured creep behavior.
A controlled comparison of enhanced-interface and diminished-interface coatings can test whether interface state correlates with creep resistance.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in steady-state creep rate and a delayed onset of tertiary creep in enhanced-interface samples would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis treats solute enrichment or segregation as beneficial, but the mediator calls this state 'chemical uniformity.' Segregation/enrichment ordinarily denotes chemical nonuniformity. The baseline and mechanism also alternate between chemical disorder, reduced uniformity, and less chemically uniform interfaces, leaving the intended beneficial chemical state internally inconsistent.
